strengths: The paper identifies two genuine, under-explored problems specific to multi-task GRPO post-training: (i) the GRPO objective evaluates to zero both when all rollouts are correct and when all are incorrect, making it an unreliable signal for task reweighting (a task that fails completely looks identical to one that is solved); and (ii) task-dependent zero-advantage rates skew effective gradient contributions away from intended task weights. The second observation, and the ratio-preserving sampler designed to fix it, is a practical contribution beyond standard DRO/group-robust methods.

The theoretical treatment is careful: the derivation of the induced ℓ1 regularizer Ω(z) via a min-flow argument (Appendix B.1), the softmax gradient for the weight update (B.2), and the improvement-aware update derived from a per-step minimax problem with a first-order Taylor approximation (B.3) are coherent and transparently presented.

The paper is honest about degenerate dynamics of strict worst-task optimization (Figure 2's weight collapse) and empirically compares the proposed improvement-aware updates against an ℓ2-regularized reward-only alternative (Appendix E, Figures 10-11), rather than only presenting the final method favorably.

Experiments include both a controlled 3-task setting and a 9-task setting, ablations of the RP sampler and acceptance-aware sampling (Figure 8), weight-dynamics analysis (Figure 6), and an efficiency analysis (steps to reach worst-task thresholds), giving reasonable mechanistic insight into why the method works.

The λ trade-off behaves as designed across experiments (increasing λ improves worst-task accuracy while reducing average accuracy), supporting the claim that robustness/average trade-off is controllable.
weaknesses: Scale and diversity of evaluation are limited: a single 3B model (Qwen-2.5-3B) post-trained on three synthetic task families (Countdown, Zebra, string-ARC) from ReasoningGym, 720 training steps. There is no evidence on standard reasoning benchmarks (math, code) or larger models, so the claimed benefit for 'general-purpose reasoners' is extrapolated well beyond what is tested.

No seed variance or statistical uncertainty is reported anywhere. RL post-training is notoriously run-sensitive; the headline gains (6-28% worst-task improvement) are single-run point estimates from bar charts, and the difference between MT-GRPO_0.2 and MT-GRPO_0.25 (58.4 vs 58.8) suggests sensitivity that cannot be assessed without repeated runs.

Missing important baselines: FAMO [11] is cited as the source of the improvement signal and the theoretical framework (Proposition 3.1 is invoked from Liu et al.), yet FAMO itself is never compared. Likewise, there is no baseline of uniform task weights combined with the RP sampler, which would isolate how much of the gain comes from reweighting versus simply fixing the zero-gradient sampling skew.

There is a tension between the core criticism and the method: the paper argues J_GRPO is an unreliable reweighting signal because it is zero both when a task is fully solved and fully failed, yet the improvement term I_k^(t) is defined as the change in J_GRPO,k and J_k(θt) in practice is the batch reward. The degree to which improvement signals computed on a zero-degenerate loss remain informative is not analyzed.

Some implementation details are unclear or questionable: improvements 'clipped to {0.1, 0.2} for stability' (Appendix D) is ambiguously specified; the filtering strategy differs between Experiments 1 and 2, complicating cross-experiment comparisons; the λ used in experiments (0.1-1.2) does not have a clearly documented mapping to the ε in the theoretical objective.
No code is actually provided (the 'Code:' field in the abstract is empty), which weakens reproducibility despite fairly detailed hyperparameter reporting.

The worst-task metric in Experiment 2 is dominated by Zebra-hard across all methods, so the 9-task results largely reflect behavior on a single hardest task; a more granular analysis of per-task Pareto behavior would strengthen the claims.

The constrained-objective formulation (Equation 4) with pairwise disparity constraints is motivating framing, but the actual algorithm optimizes a heuristic surrogate (single gradient step on a softmax-parameterized weighting with an improvement term); the connection between theory and practice is looser than the presentation suggests.

strengths: The paper identifies genuine and previously under-discussed problems specific to GRPO-style multi-task post-training: (i) varying zero-advantage (zero-gradient) rates across tasks skew effective gradient contributions away from intended task weights, and (ii) the GRPO loss cannot distinguish 'all-correct' from 'all-wrong' prompts, making it unreliable as a weight-update signal. These observations are well-motivated and supported empirically (Figures 1, 2, 3).

The proposed algorithm is a coherent combination of ideas: improvement-aware task reweighting (decoupling weight updates from the GRPO loss), plus a ratio-preserving, acceptance-aware sampler that enforces target task proportions in the post-filtered batch. The sampler (Algorithm 2) is a concrete, practical contribution.

The experimental section includes useful component-level ablations: MT-GRPO with vs. without RP SAMPLER (Figure 8), with vs. without acceptance-aware sampling, and improvement-aware vs. regularized reward-only reweighting (Appendix E, Figures 10-11). Weight dynamics (Figure 6) provide mechanistic insight into why the method works.

The derivation of the induced L1 regularizer from the Lagrangian formulation (Appendix B.1) and the connection of the improvement-aware update to a minimax objective (Appendix B.3) are worked out in reasonable detail, and the lambda trade-off behavior matches the intended design across both experiments.

Reproducibility information is reasonably complete: model, training framework (verl), GPU setup, rollout counts, optimizer settings, sampler hyperparameters, and reward protocol are all specified (Appendix D), and datasets are publicly released (ReasoningGym).
weaknesses: Limited scale and task diversity undermine the central claim about 'reliable LLM reasoning across tasks.' All experiments use Qwen-2.5-3B on three synthetic task families from ReasoningGym (Countdown, Zebra, ARC) with only 720 training steps. There is no evidence the gains transfer to realistic, heterogeneous task suites (e.g., math, code, structured reasoning as cited in the introduction), leaving the general-purpose framing of Section 1 largely unsupported.

No statistical rigor: results appear to be single-seed, with no error bars, confidence intervals, or variance analysis. Worst-task accuracy is the minimum over only 3 (or 9) noisy accuracy estimates, so the headline differences (e.g., 6 points over DAPO) could plausibly be within run-to-run variance for RL post-training.

The efficiency claim ('50% fewer training steps to reach 50% worst-task accuracy') is narrowly scoped (one threshold, one setting) and ignores the additional rollout compute consumed by the RP sampler (oversampling factor Mos = 3 and up to 10 resampling rounds). No wall-clock or FLOP accounting is provided, so the claimed efficiency gain may be overstated.

Missing relevant baselines: despite an extensive related-work section citing multi-task RL post-training methods (e.g., [72], [75], [76], [5]) and gradient-conflict/reweighting methods (FAMO [11], PCGrad [7]), the comparison set is limited to GRPO/DAPO and SEC variants. Simple alternatives, such as fixed non-uniform sampling, reward normalization across tasks, or a DRO-style weight update without the improvement term, are not compared against directly in the main results.

Internal inconsistencies raise concerns about care: Section 6 states '10k training instances' per level while Appendix D states '1000 training instances'; Section 5 refers to 'task weights from Subroutine 2' where Subroutine 1 is meant; and there is tension between the paper's own argument that the GRPO loss is an unreliable performance signal (Section 3.1) and its use of the GRPO-loss difference I_k^(t) (Equation 8) as the improvement signal.

The lambda hyperparameter must be selected differently per experiment (0.2-0.25 for 3 tasks, 0.1-1.2 for 9 tasks), and in Experiment 2 the larger-lambda configurations that achieve the best worst-task accuracy (61.7) do so at a substantial cost in average accuracy (63.9 vs. DAPO's 69.5). The practical guidance for choosing lambda, and whether the robustness/average trade-off is favorable relative to simply running DAPO, is not clearly established.

The theoretical analysis is largely derivational rather than providing guarantees; the improvement-aware update is justified via a first-order Taylor argument whose validity (small step size) is assumed rather than verified, and the 'formal analysis' referenced in Section B.3 for preventing weight collapse is heuristic.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely novel and practically important issue specific to GRPO-based multi-task post-training: prompts yielding zero advantages (zero gradients) are unevenly distributed across tasks, so naively upweighting weak tasks fails to translate into actual gradient contributions. This observation, and the ratio-preserving sampler (Algorithm 2) that corrects it, is a concrete and sensible contribution beyond standard DRO/group-robustness reweighting.

The problem is well-motivated and cleanly formalized: the constrained formulation (Eq. 4) with a Lagrangian-derived regularizer (Section B.1, including a correct minimum-flow derivation giving the L1 regularizer) provides a principled framing, and the observation that the GRPO loss is unreliable as a weight-update signal (all-correct vs all-incorrect rollouts) is a real insight not present in prior robust-optimization work.

The empirical study is reasonably thorough: two settings (3-task controlled and 9-task scaled), four sensible baselines (GRPO, DAPO, and SEC curriculum variants), analysis of weight dynamics (Fig. 6), steps-to-threshold efficiency analysis (Fig. 5), and ablations covering each component (RP sampler, acceptance-aware sampling, and regularized reward-only reweighting vs. improvement-aware reweighting in Appendix E).

The improvement-aware reweighting signal is derived from a first-order minimax argument (Section B.3) that connects per-step improvement to gradient inner products, and the paper honestly analyzes why pure worst-task optimization collapses (Figure 2) and why regularization alone is insufficient (Appendix E), which strengthens the design justification.
weaknesses: Scale and generality of evaluation are limited: all experiments use Qwen-2.5-3B on synthetic ReasoningGym tasks (Countdown, Zebra, string-ARC) with only 200 test instances per level and, apparently, no repeated seeds or variance/confidence reporting. Given noisy RL post-training, single-run comparisons at ~5-point accuracy gaps are hard to assess; the headline '16–28%' improvement also conflates numbers across two different experiment settings.

Internal inconsistency in dataset description: the main text (Section 6) states '10k training instances' per level while Appendix D states '1000 training instances and 200 test instances.' This kind of discrepancy undermines confidence in experimental reporting and reproducibility.

Compute accounting for the efficiency claim is incomplete. The '50% fewer training steps' claim does not account for the extra rollout generation cost of the RP sampler (oversampling factor M_os = 3, up to 10 resampling rounds, plus rollouts discarded by zero-gradient filtering), so the effective gradient-compute comparison against baselines is unclear.

The improvement signal I_k is defined via the GRPO loss (Eq. 8), yet the paper itself argues the GRPO loss is an unreliable task-performance signal; the paper does not reconcile this tension (reliability for weight updates vs. performance measurement). Additionally, improvements are estimated from a single training batch, which is high-variance, and the clipped range {0.1, 0.2} is unusual and under-justified.

The λ trade-off parameter must be chosen per experiment (0.2/0.25 in Exp. 1; 0.1–1.2 in Exp. 2), and the worst-task/average trade-off is somewhat expected for any worst-case-oriented method; no guidance is given for selecting λ in new settings. Comparisons with other multi-task RL post-training approaches beyond SEC/DAPO (e.g., cross-dataset reward normalization [72], mixture methods [5, 71]) are absent.

The theoretical development in B.3 closely follows FAMO (Liu et al. [11]) machinery with first-order approximations; it is a derivation rather than a new guarantee, and no convergence or robustness analysis for the full MT-GRPO algorithm (including the RP sampler's biasing of batch composition) is provided.
There is no explicit limitations section, and the code link in the abstract is empty, weakening reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameters in Appendix D.

strengths: The paper identifies a real, well-motivated, and underexplored problem: standard GRPO post-training on task mixtures leads to imbalanced outcomes because (i) the average objective permits compensating one task with another, and (ii) zero-advantage prompts contribute no gradient, so effective gradient contributions deviate from intended task weights even when weights are explicitly set. The GRPO-specific nature of these issues (advantage-based losses being unreliable for reweighting) is articulated clearly and distinguishes the work from prior DRO/multi-task reweighting.

The method is developed in a principled way: the constrained disparity objective is reformulated via Lagrangian duality, the induced regularizer Ω(z) is derived exactly (nice min-flow argument showing it reduces to an ℓ1 penalty), the degenerate weight-collapse behavior of strict worst-task maximization is diagnosed and analyzed, and the improvement-aware update is derived from a first-order minimax surrogate (Appendix C.3) rather than presented as an ad hoc heuristic.

The two identified failure modes are each addressed by a dedicated mechanism (improvement-aware weight update; ratio-preserving sampler with acceptance-aware resampling), and the ablation study (Figures 10–12, 16) convincingly isolates the contribution of each component, including diagnostics showing the assigned-weight vs. realized-batch-ratio mismatch for ARC that the RPS is designed to fix.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: three controlled settings (3 tasks, 9 tasks, 7B models on heterogeneous MATH/ARC/SciKnowEval plus OLMo-3 7B), competitive baselines (GRPO, SEC-GRPO, DAPO, SEC-DAPO), a sequential-training comparison with forgetting analysis, a λ-controlled trade-off analysis, and an honest wall-clock analysis showing a ~10% per-step overhead but faster convergence in real time (Table 1, Figure 18).

Reproducibility is strong: code is released, and Appendix E provides full training details (optimizers, batch sizes, rollout counts, hyperparameters including λ, η, oversampling factors, and dataset construction). Limitations (verifiable rewards only, robustness to out-of-mixture tasks) are candidly discussed.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than high. Minimax/DRO-style group reweighting, improvement-based reweighting (Liu et al., 2023), and acceptance-aware/oversampling batch construction are all established ideas; the contribution is their careful adaptation to the GRPO post-training setting. The zero-advantage ambiguity observation is a genuinely useful insight, but the overall algorithm is an incremental combination of known mechanisms.

There is no evidence of multiple seeds or variance reporting: all training curves and headline numbers appear to come from single runs. Given the noisy nature of RL post-training and the fairly small worst-task gaps in some settings (e.g., Experiment 2 where MT-GRO variants span 40.4–46.3%), the reliability of the reported differences is hard to assess.

Task-level rewards J_k and per-step improvements I_k are estimated from training batches (with improvements clipped to {0.1, 0.2} for stability), and the weight-update learning rate (1e-4/1e-5), η, and λ all appear to require tuning. The method introduces several hyperparameters whose sensitivity is only partially characterized, which may limit out-of-the-box applicability.

The worst-task metric inherently favors the proposed objective, and the cost is visible: in the 9-task setting MT-GRO's average accuracy (61.7–66.0 for λ ≥ 0.3) trails DAPO (69.5), and negative relative change on easy tasks occurs for larger λ. The trade-off is acknowledged and controlled by λ, but practitioners seeking average performance gain less from this method.

Some experimental comparability concerns: Experiment 1 uses a strict DAPO filtering strategy while Experiment 2 uses a more lenient one, and rollout counts differ (72 vs. 8); the effect of these choices on cross-experiment conclusions is not analyzed. Related recent multi-task RL works (e.g., Omnikinker, MedGRPO, Wu et al. 2025b) are cited but not compared empirically.

All evaluation is limited to verifiable rewards and relatively short training runs (150–720 steps) on 3B/7B models; the paper itself acknowledges that reliability of the reweighting mechanism in non-verifiable domains is open.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes two genuinely underexplored issues in multi-task GRPO post-training: the unreliability of GRPO losses (which saturate to similar values when rollouts are all correct/incorrect) as signals for task reweighting, and the divergence between intended task weights and realized gradient contributions due to heterogeneous zero-gradient rates (Figure 3). The motivation and diagnosis of these issues are convincing.

The theoretical development is mostly clean: the Lagrangian reformulation of the constrained problem (Section C.1) yields a closed-form induced ℓ1 regularizer via a flow argument, and the improvement-aware update rule is derived from a first-order minimax approximation (Section C.3) rather than presented as an ad-hoc heuristic.

The empirical study is unusually thorough for this area: an ablation isolating the two components (IWU vs. RPS, Figures 10-12), a nine-task scaling experiment, comparison against sequential training with two orderings and forgetting analysis (Figure 15), sensitivity to λ, and a wall-clock analysis accounting for the ~10% per-step overhead of the ratio-preserving sampler (Table 1, Figure 19). Code and detailed hyperparameters are provided.
The honest limitations section correctly notes the reliance on verifiable rewards and the open question of robustness to tasks outside the training mixture.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. Both components are adaptations of well-known ideas—minimax/DRO task reweighting (Sagawa et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023) and curriculum/data-rebalancing—to the GRPO setting. The strongest empirical competitor (SEC-GRPO/SEC-DAPO) already implements advantage-based task weighting, so the delta over prior work is primarily the improvement signal and the ratio-preserving sampler. This is a useful but incremental contribution.

The evaluation is confined to small models (3B/7B), verifiable-reward tasks, small test sets (200 instances per task), and relatively few training steps (150-720). Whether worst-task gains persist at larger scale or transfer to held-out tasks is not demonstrated, which limits the significance of the 'general-purpose reliability' framing.

The worst-task vs. average trade-off is largely inherent: in Experiment 2, MT-GRPO variants score 61.7-66.0 average accuracy versus DAPO's 69.5, and per-difficulty relative change shows meaningful regressions on easy tasks for larger λ. The method provides a knob rather than a Pareto improvement, and λ requires per-setting tuning (different values, e.g., 0.05/0.2/1.2, are selected across experiments).

Some reporting choices are favorable to the method: in Experiment 3, results are reported 'at each method's best worst-task step rather than the final training step' (Figure 9), a selection protocol not applied uniformly everywhere; the abstract's headline of '16-28%' improvement is against the weakest baseline (GRPO), while the margin over the stronger DAPO baseline is smaller (~6%).

There are no convergence or robustness guarantees for the alternating weight/policy scheme; the saddle-point derivation replaces hard disparity constraints with a restricted inner minimization over Δ_K, an approximation whose effect is not quantified theoretically. The method also introduces several new hyperparameters (λ, η, oversampling factor, resampling cap, inflation cap) whose sensitivity is only partially explored.

The theoretical 'restricting to Δ_K' and softmax-parameterized updates appear somewhat disconnected from the final algorithm, which uses a momentum-like regularized logit update plus improvement clipping {0.1, 0.2}; the gap between the derived objective and the implemented procedure weakens the link between the analysis and the empirical results.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: multi-task RL post-training with GRPO suffers from task imbalance and, crucially, task-dependent zero-gradient rates that decouple intended task weights from realized gradient contributions — a limitation specific to RL post-training that prior DRO/multi-task work does not address. This is a genuinely relevant observation for the field.

The method is developed carefully rather than proposed ad hoc: the constrained objective is derived via a Lagrangian reformulation (Appendix C.1 gives a clean closed form for the induced l1 regularizer), the degenerate dynamics of strict worst-task reweighting are analyzed, and the improvement-aware update is derived from a first-order minimax approximation (Appendix C.3). The rationale for each design choice (IWU, RP sampler, acceptance-aware sampling) is explained and empirically motivated (Figures 2, 3, 12, 16).

Comprehensive evaluation: three experimental scales (3 tasks, 9 tasks, 7B models on MATH/ARC/SciKnowEval plus OLMo-3 7B), comparison against GRPO, SEC-GRPO, DAPO, SEC-DAPO, and sequential training baselines, an ablation isolating IWU vs. RP sampler (Section D.2), sensitivity analysis over the trade-off parameter lambda, regularization-only ablations (Appendix F), and a wall-clock analysis showing the ~10% per-step overhead is outweighed by faster convergence (Table 1, Figure 19).

Honest limitations section acknowledging that robustness to tasks outside the mixture and non-verifiable reward domains remain open, plus released code and detailed hyperparameters, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: No variance reporting: all results appear to come from single training runs. RL post-training is notoriously high-variance, and several claimed gains (e.g., 6% worst-task improvement in Experiment 2; the ranking of MT-GRPO_0.3 vs. DAPO in average accuracy) could be sensitive to seed. Without multiple seeds or confidence intervals, the reliability of some comparisons is hard to assess.

The evaluation relies exclusively on verifiable, largely synthetic tasks from ReasoningGym/Chen et al. (2025b). It remains unclear whether improvement-aware reweighting transfers to natural benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K/HumanEval-style mixes) or to non-verifiable rewards, which limits the practical reach of the contribution despite the acknowledged limitation.

The contribution is a composition of existing ideas — DRO-style worst-group reweighting, improvement-based weighting (Liu et al., 2023), and curriculum/sampling mechanisms — adapted to GRPO. The adaptation is non-trivial (particularly the zero-gradient rate issue), but the overall novelty is moderate; a sharper comparison against closely related multi-task RL works cited in related work (e.g., Wu et al., 2025b; Feng et al., 2025; MedGRPO) is not provided.

Method sensitivity: performance depends materially on lambda (average accuracy drops noticeably at large lambda, e.g., 61.7 vs. 69.5 in Experiment 2), and the improvement signal I_k is a one-step, first-order surrogate that may be noisy; the paper provides ablations but no analysis of robustness of these choices to different step sizes or batch sizes.

Some reported baselines results are inconsistent in framing: in Experiment 2 the strongest average accuracy belongs to DAPO/SEC-DAPO, and MT-GRPO's advantage is confined to worst-task accuracy and relative change on hard tasks; the paper should be more explicit that the method trades average performance for robustness in some regimes.
